Empirical Research Plan – Social (External) Returns to Education in U.S. States, 1960-1980  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Two–stage least squares (IV) exploiting cross-state / cross-cohort changes in compulsory-schooling and child-labor laws.  
Why IV?  
• Endogenous regressor = average education of peers in the state-of-birth × cohort cell (Ā_sct).  
• Laws shifted schooling exogenously for cohorts exposed in a given state but were orthogonal to contemporaneous labour-market demand shocks four decades later.  
• The interaction of laws with state and cohort provides quasi-random, plausibly exogenous variation in Ā_sct that is not chosen by individuals or contemporaneous firms, satisfying the relevance + exclusion conditions better than DID alone.  

Design in one sentence: Use state-of-birth × cohort variation in compulsory-attendance ages as instruments for leave-one-out average education of the cohort, while controlling for each worker’s own schooling, to estimate the spillover effect of peers’ education on his wage.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
T_sct  ≡  Ā_sct = average years of schooling of men aged 40–49 in Census year t who were born in state s and cohort c (c = year-of-birth). We use a leave-one-out mean to purge the individual’s own education:  

Ā_{–i,sct} = ( Σ_{j≠i} Edu_j ) / (N_sct – 1).

Continuous treatment; units = years.

Instrument(s)  
Z₁_sct = Predicted average compelled schooling years based on the compulsory-attendance age in state s when cohort c reached compulsory-schooling age.  
Z₂_sct = Predicted reduction in legal work years from child-labor law in state s for cohort c.  
Main first-stage: Ā_sct = π₁ Z₁_sct + π₂ Z₂_sct + controls + u.

Control group & counterfactual  
Cohorts/states not exposed (or less exposed) to higher compulsory ages in their school years act as the counterfactual for cohorts/states that were exposed. Because the laws vary both across states and time, each state serves as its own control across cohorts, and each cohort faces multiple states with different legal environments.

Timing  
Exposure year = year-of-birth + 6 (approx. school entry). A cohort is “treated” if, at that age, the state had already legislated a higher compulsory-attendance age / stricter child-labor law.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Relevance: Compulsory-schooling laws significantly raise average education in the affected state-cohort cell.  
– Plausible; shown repeatedly in prior work, but we will present F-statistics >10.

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on (i) own education, (ii) state-of-birth fixed effects, (iii) cohort fixed effects, and (iv) Census-year fixed effects, the only channel through which the laws affect an individual’s log wage four decades later is via the schooling of his peers (Ā_sct).  
– Plausibility: Laws were enacted decades earlier and should not directly affect contemporary labour-demand shocks. Remaining concern: laws could have affected school quality or other policies; we address in Section 4.

A3. Independence (Ignorability): Conditional on FE, the timing of state legal changes is uncorrelated with other unobserved, long-run wage determinants specific to the birth cohort.  
– Plausible after conditioning on state × year trends and pre-trend tests.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-state contamination): Education spillovers are mainly within state-of-birth cohorts; interstate spillovers are small.  
– Potentially violated by migration; mitigation discussed below.

A5. Monotonicity: Higher compulsory-attendance age weakly increases years of schooling for all affected individuals.  
– Reasonable for mandatory schooling.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Remedies  

Threat 1: Selective Migration  
– If educated individuals leave their birth state, Ā_sct measured in birth state may mis-proxy actual peer exposure.  
Remedies:  
a) Use state of birth rather than state of residence to define both treatment and instrument, breaking the link between migration choices and contemporaneous wages.  
b) Show robustness restricting to non-movers (state of birth = state of residence) in subsample.  
c) Instrument balance check: Test whether laws predicted migration rates.

Threat 2: Mechanical reflection / “own-education” bias  
– Individual education enters both dependent variable and (un-adjusted) group mean.  
Remedies:  
a) Leave-one-out mean (Ā_{–i,sct}).  
b) Include own education as control in second stage.  
c) Show robustness with jackknife IV à la Angrist & Pischke (2009).

Threat 3: Law changes correlated with long-run state growth trends  
– A reforming state might already be on a higher growth trajectory.  
Remedies:  
a) Include state-of-birth × linear cohort trend.  
b) Control for contemporaneous state GDP per capita in Census year.  
c) Event-study graphs of wages around law changes to check for pre-trends (placebo leads).

------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # for 2SLS with fixed effects
library(ivreg)       # robustness
library(sandwich)    # clustered SEs
library(lmtest)

# 1. Load data
# Assume files: census60.csv, census70.csv, census80.csv, laws.csv
c60 <- fread("census60.csv")
c70 <- fread("census70.csv")
c80 <- fread("census80.csv")
laws <- fread("laws.csv")   # state, year, comp_age, childlabor_age

# 2. Stack Census files
census <- rbindlist(list(c60, c70, c80), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

# 3. Keep sample: men 40–49
census <- census[sex=="male" & age>=40 & age<=49]

# 4. Key variables
census[, yob  := year_birth]                       # supplied
census[, cohort := yob]                            # alias
census[, state  := state_birth]                    # state of birth
census[, cyear  := census_year]                    # 1960, 1970, 1980
census[, lnwage:= log(weekly_wage)]                # outcome
census[, edu   := years_education]

# 5. Merge laws – compute legal exposure for each cohort
# First collapse laws to year of reform
setkey(laws, state, year)
# For each individual, find the compulsory age & child-labor age in force
# when he was age 6 (school entry)
census[, exposure_year := yob + 6]
census <- laws[census, on = .(state, year<=exposure_year),
               mult = "last", allow.cartesian = TRUE]

# 6. Compute instruments: compelled years of schooling
# Simple measure: max(0, comp_age - 6)
census[, comp_years := pmax(0, comp_age - 6)]
census[, cl_years   := pmax(0, childlabor_age - 14)]  # example

# 7. Create state×cohort averages & leave-one-out mean
census[, avg_edu := mean(edu), by = .(state, cohort, cyear)]
census[, N       := .N,        by = .(state, cohort, cyear)]
census[, lo_avg  := (avg_edu*N - edu)/(N-1)]          # leave-one-out

# 8. Instruments aggregated to cell (consistent with 1st stage)
census[, Z1 := mean(comp_years), by = .(state, cohort)]
census[, Z2 := mean(cl_years)  , by = .(state, cohort)]

# 9. MAIN 2SLS
iv_formula <- lnwage ~ edu + lo_avg | edu + Z1 + Z2
# FE: state + cohort + cyear
model_iv <- feols(iv_formula,
                  data = census,
                  cluster = ~state,
                  fixef = ~state + cohort + cyear)
etable(model_iv, se = "cluster")

# 10. First-stage F-statistic
wald(model_iv, ~lo_avg)

# 11. Robustness: restrict to non-movers
nonmovers <- census[state == state_residence]
model_nm <- feols(iv_formula, data = nonmovers,
                  cluster = ~state, fixef = ~state+cohort+cyear)
etable(list(Main=model_iv, NonMovers=model_nm), se = "cluster")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  

Theory (Lucas, Moretti) predicts a positive externality: being surrounded by more educated workers raises individual wages. U.S. metropolitan studies typically find an elasticity of 1–2% higher wages per additional year of average schooling among peers. Given our broader state-level measure (more spatial dilution), I expect:

Spillover coefficient β ≈ 0.01 – 0.015  
(i.e., a 1-year increase in average schooling in one’s birth-state cohort raises an individual’s wage by about 1–1.5%), statistically significant at conventional levels if externalities exist.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)

C1: Instrument strongly correlated with endogenous regressor (F-stat >10)… 1  
C2: Instrument affects outcome only through endogenous regressor (exclusion)… 0.5  
C3: No omitted variables correlated with instrument across state×cohort… 0.5  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers)… 1  
C5: Proper clustering / inference… 1  

Total = 4 / 5. Remaining concerns lie mainly with the exclusion and independence assumptions, both partially but not fully testable; robustness exercises aim to bolster credibility.
